slides.title: Hook
slides.body_html:
The deployed surface — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral — is a thin product layer on top of a single class of artefact: a decoder-only transformer pretrained on internet-scale text against a next-token-prediction objective, then post-trained against a human-preference signal.

The product layer is not the artefact. This talk specifies the artefact, then specifies the product layer, then names the gap between them.

faces_html.general:
You have talked to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or one of their siblings. They wrote your code, summarised your meeting, told you why your soup is too salty.

They feel like they understand you.

None of them does. Underneath, every one of them is a probability calculator that emits one word at a time. The rest is engineering and scale.

This talk takes the calculator apart.

slides.title: Chatbot Interactions
slides.body_html:
Three examples of the surface.

Ask: "How do I get the disk usage of subdirectories on Linux?" Get: du -sh */ | sort -h, with a clear gloss of what each flag does.

Ask: "Walk me through Bayes' theorem with a medical-test example." Get: a clean derivation with the prior/likelihood/ posterior labelled.

Ask: "Translate this Korean sign for me." Get: a translation, a guess at where the sign was photographed, and a caveat about the translation's confidence.

Three domains. Three formats. One machine. And the machine has no idea what disk usage is, no idea what Bayes' theorem is, no idea what Korean is.

It is doing exactly one thing.

slides.title: Next Token Predictor
slides.body_html:
A modern LLM parameterises a conditional distribution $p_\theta(x_{n+1} \mid x_{\le n})$ over a finite vocabulary $V$. Inference is auto-regressive: sample (or take argmax) $x_{n+1} \sim p_\theta(\cdot \mid x_{\le n})$, append, re-evaluate.

The conditional distribution is computed by a single forward pass through the network. The network is fixed; the input is the prefix. Decoding strategy (greedy, top-$k$, top-$p$, temperature, beam search) sits outside the model — it is a sampling choice, not a model choice.

Everything that follows specifies the network that computes $p_\theta$.

faces_html.general:
The one thing the machine does:

Take a chunk of text. Compute a probability for every word that might come next. Pick one (usually the most likely, sometimes a slightly less likely one for variety). Append it. Repeat.

The text "I am writing a" might produce a probability distribution where "letter" gets 8%, "book" gets 5%, "report" gets 4%, and a long tail of less likely options share the rest. Sample. Pick "letter." The new chunk is "I am writing a letter," fed back into the same machine, which now computes a distribution over what follows that. And so on.

Every paragraph you have ever read from a chatbot was built this way. One word at a time. No outline, no plan, no structure beyond what the next-word probabilities compel.

The mechanical core. After this card, the audience knows what an

The "I am writing a..." example is concrete and falsifiable —
the audience could imagine running it themselves. That is
deliberate; abstract probability claims are easier to dismiss.

Technical face introduces the formal object and isolates
decoding strategy as separate. This matters for the alignment
card later (post-training changes p, not the decoding).

slides.title: Autoregression
slides.body_html:
Auto-regressive decoding has two consequences worth naming explicitly.

  1. Causal masking in attention enforces that position $i$ attends only to positions $j \le i$. The model is structurally unable to look ahead; the loss can be computed by a single forward pass over the full sequence.
  2. No revision pass. Inference cost is $O(n)$ forward passes for $n$ tokens (with KV caching). The model does not iterate; the apparent coherence is a property of the conditional distribution, not of a planning procedure.

Modern systems (chain-of-thought, agentic loops) add planning outside the model — multiple forward passes that sample, inspect, and re-prompt. The base model still does not plan.

faces_html.general:
Two implications of the one-word-at-a-time rule.

The model cannot revise. Once a word has been emitted, it is in the prefix. The model cannot look at what it just said and decide it was wrong. It can only condition on it.

The model cannot plan. It has no sense of where the paragraph is heading until it has typed it. The appearance of structure — paragraphs, arguments, jokes with payoffs — comes from the fact that, given a strong prefix, the most likely next words are also the words that continue the structure.

The structure is encoded in the prefix's continuation probabilities, not in any plan the model held.

slides.title: Ntp Summary
slides.body_html: Beat 2 closes. The artefact under examination is $p_\theta(x_{n+1} \mid x_{\le n})$ deployed under auto-regressive sampling. The remaining beats specify the function class $p_\theta$ belongs to and the procedure that fits $\theta$.

faces_html.general:
Half of the thesis, named.

A modern LLM is a sequential probability calculator. It does not understand. It does not plan. It does not revise. It samples one word at a time from a distribution it computes from the prefix.

The distribution is the whole game. The next thirty minutes are about how that distribution gets computed.

Beat-2 closer. One slide. Names what the audience now believes

The line "the distribution is the whole game" is the load-

follows is in service of computing this one distribution.

slides.title: Mechanisms Overview
slides.body_html:
The mechanism stack of a decoder-only transformer:

  1. Tokeniser $\tau: \text{bytes} \to V^*$.
  2. Embedding $e: V \to \mathbb{R}^d$, parameterised by $W_E \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}$, with positional encoding added.
  3. Attention layer, multi-head: $\text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_h})\, V$, causally masked.
  4. Transformer block: attention + MLP, both residual, with layer norm. Stack $L$ of them ($L=12$ for GPT-2 small, $L \ge 80$ for frontier models).
  5. Unembedding $W_U$ followed by softmax to yield the next-token distribution.

Plus the training procedure that fits the parameters; that is its own beat.

Each of items 1-4 is a card.

faces_html.general:
Predicting the next word does not, by itself, sound impressive. "Statistical fluency" is decades old.

What is new is that the prediction is good enough to feel like understanding. That is the load-bearing claim of modern machine learning, and it took four ideas, stacked, to get there.

  1. Tokenisation — convert text into numerical chunks.
  2. Embedding — give every chunk a position in space, where distance and direction encode meaning.
  3. Attention — let chunks read each other, so a word's contribution depends on its neighbours.
  4. The transformer block — repeat the read-and-mix many times, so meaning compounds across layers.

Plus a fifth: training at scale. We will get to that in beat 5.

slides.title: Tokenisation
slides.body_html:
The tokeniser is a function $\tau: \text{bytes} \to V^*$ that maps a byte string to a sequence of integer ids over a fixed vocabulary $V$. Sub-word algorithms (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) are the working compromise: bounded vocabulary size, no out-of-vocabulary failures, common words are single tokens, rare words split into known pieces.

$|V|$ is a design constant chosen before training (50,257 for GPT-2, ~100k for modern frontier models). The model is defined on $V^*$, not on text. Everything downstream operates on sequences of integers in $[0, |V|-1]$.

Token boundaries can affect behaviour in non-obvious ways (tokens split across visual word boundaries, multi-byte characters, capitalisation). For this talk, the relevant fact is just: there is a fixed alphabet of about 50,000 symbols, and the model's job is to predict the next symbol in that alphabet.

faces_html.general:
The model cannot read text. It can read numbers.

So before anything else, text gets cut into pieces, and each piece gets a number.

The pieces are not characters and not whole words. They are something in between, called tokens. The word "tokenisation" might become four tokens: "token," "is," "ation," and a space marker. Common words are single tokens; rare words and typos get split into smaller pieces.

A token vocabulary has on the order of 50,000 entries. Every piece of text the model has ever seen, and every piece it will ever produce, is built from those 50,000 building blocks.

From here on, when we say "the model reads," we mean: it reads a sequence of integers, each one indexing into the vocabulary.

slides.title: Embedding
slides.body_html:
The embedding layer is a learned lookup table $W_E \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}$, with $d = 768$ for GPT-2 small (and larger for bigger models). Token id $i$ indexes row $i$, yielding a $d$-dimensional vector.

Embedding lifts the model from a function over $V^*$ (discrete) to a function over $(\mathbb{R}^d)^*$ (continuous). All downstream operations — attention, MLP, unembedding — are continuous functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued sequences.

Positional information is added separately (positional embedding, rotary, etc.) so the model can distinguish "cat chases dog" from "dog chases cat."

The geometry of $W_E$ is not designed; it is what gradient descent on the next-token prediction loss picks out. The next card discusses what that geometry looks like.

faces_html.general:
Tokens are integers. Integers are not useful — you cannot do "this integer is somewhat similar to that integer" with raw indices.

So the next step gives every token a position in a high- dimensional space. Imagine a 768-dimensional graph, with one point per token in the vocabulary. Token "cat" is one point. Token "dog" is another. Token "thermodynamics" is another.

The position is a list of 768 numbers — the embedding of that token.

Two tokens are similar if their points are close together. Two tokens are related by some pattern if the line between them points in a particular direction.

This is the trick that makes everything else work. The model cannot operate on integers, but it can do arithmetic on high-dimensional points. So we lift integers into points, and the integers' relationships become geometry.

General face uses the "graph with one point per token" framing.
Technical face introduces W_E and notes that geometry is

Note: I am not introducing positional embedding as a separate

slides.title: Embedding Geometry
slides.body_html:
Two empirical properties of trained embedding spaces:

Local clustering. Cosine similarity between embeddings is a usable proxy for token-level semantic similarity. This is the basis for vector-search applications (retrieval, RAG) that use LLM embeddings as features.

Linear directional structure. Some semantic relations correspond approximately to fixed offsets: $e(\text{king}) - e(\text{man}) + e(\text{woman}) \approx e(\text{queen})$. The relation is approximate (it depends heavily on the embedding model; GPT-2 raw token embeddings are noisier than older word2vec/GloVe embeddings) but the pattern is robust enough to use pedagogically and load-bearing for the talk.

Caveat: the directional structure exists in $W_E$ and in the residual stream at deeper layers; the deeper-layer directional structure is closer to "concept-of-X" than to "token-of-X."

faces_html.general:
What does the geometry actually look like?

Clusters. Animal words end up near each other. Verbs end up near each other. Country names end up near each other. The model was never told that "cat" and "dog" are similar; it figured out a representation in which they end up close, because their similarity helps prediction.

Directions. The vector from "Paris" to "France" points in roughly the same direction as the vector from "Berlin" to "Germany." There is a "capital-of-country" direction, and you can travel along it. (king - man + woman lands near queen — the famous demonstration of this property.)

No one wrote down "make capitals offset from countries by a consistent vector." The model found that arrangement because it makes the next-word probabilities sharper.

The geometry is not metaphorical. The model is literally doing arithmetic on these vectors when it makes predictions.

slides.title: Attention
slides.body_html:
Attention in its scaled-dot-product form computes $\text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_h})\, V$ where $Q$, $K$, $V$ are linear projections of the input vectors. Each output position is a convex combination of the input value vectors, with weights given by the softmax-normalised query-key compatibilities.

Multi-head attention runs $h$ attention computations in parallel on $h$ orthogonal sub-spaces of the embedding (with $d_h = d/h$), then concatenates and projects back. Each head learns to attend along a different axis — syntactic position, coreference, named-entity proximity, semantic similarity — though the per-head specialisation is empirical, not mandated.

Causal masking sets the upper-triangular entries of $QK^\top$ to $-\infty$ before softmax, so each position $i$ attends only to positions $j \le i$.

faces_html.general:
Embedding gets us a static map: each token has a fixed position. But meaning isn't static. The word "bank" in "the bank of the river" is a different thing from "the bank gave me a loan." The token is the same; the meaning depends on the neighbours.

Attention is the mechanism that lets a token's representation be modified by its neighbours, during the forward pass.

Concretely: for every token in the sequence, the model computes how much each other token in the sequence is worth paying attention to. Those weights are then used to mix the other tokens' information into the current token's representation.

A token's vector enters the attention layer as one thing and leaves as something subtly different — informed by which other tokens it decided to look at, and how strongly.

Attention is the central architectural innovation of modern LLMs. It is the reason transformers replaced the previous generation of architectures. It is the reason the talk spends time on it.

slides.title: Attention Disambig
slides.body_html:
Concretely. Two sentences:

I sat on the bank of the river and watched the fish.

I went to the bank to deposit a cheque.

The token "bank" is the same. After embedding, the vector for "bank" is identical in both sentences.

After one or two attention layers, it is not.

In the first sentence, attention has pulled in information from "river" and "fish." The "bank" vector has shifted toward the part of the embedding space where geographical features live. In the second sentence, attention has pulled in information from "deposit" and "cheque," and "bank" has shifted toward the financial-institution region.

Same input. Same starting vector. Different neighbours. Different output. That is what attention does.

Run this same trick across twelve layers, on every token, looking at every other token, and you have a representation that is deeply context-aware. You also have a reason to believe that the word "understand," when applied to the machine, is doing some work — even if it is not the work the audience instinctively assumed.

slides.title: Attention Qkv
slides.body_html:
The mechanic, more precisely.

For each token in the sequence, three vectors are derived from its embedding by linear projection:

  • Query $Q = x W_Q$ — what am I looking for?
  • Key $K = x W_K$ — what do I offer?
  • Value $V = x W_V$ — what do I contribute if picked?

For a target position $i$, attention computes a weight distribution over all positions $j \le i$:

$$\alpha_{ij} = \text{softmax}_j \left( \frac{Q_i \cdot K_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}} \right)$$

The output at position $i$ is the weighted sum:

$$o_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} V_j$$

Multi-head attention runs $h$ such computations in parallel on $h$ non-overlapping $d_h$-dimensional subspaces of the $d$-dimensional embedding. Heads learn to specialise — some attend along positional axes, some along semantic axes, some along syntactic ones.

$W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, $W_O$ are the learned parameters. They constitute roughly one third of the parameters per transformer block; the other two thirds are the MLP.

slides.title: Transformer Block
slides.body_html:
A transformer block applied to the residual stream:

$$h' = h + \text{Attn}(\text{LN}(h))$$

$$h'' = h' + \text{MLP}(\text{LN}(h'))$$

The MLP is a position-wise two-layer feed-forward network with a non-linearity (typically GELU): $\text{MLP}(x) = \text{GELU}(x W_{\text{in}} + b_{\text{in}})\, W_{\text{out}} + b_{\text{out}}$, with $W_{\text{in}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 4d}$, $W_{\text{out}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4d \times d}$.

The two halves have distinct roles:

  • Attention mixes across positions (each output depends on all previous inputs).
  • MLP mixes across features at a single position (each output depends only on the corresponding input).

The combination is what makes transformers expressive. A pure attention model has no per-position non-linearity; a pure MLP model has no positional mixing. Both are needed.

faces_html.general:
Attention is half of the work in each layer. The other half is a small neural network — called an MLP, multi-layer perceptron — that operates on each token independently, after attention has done its mixing.

The clean way to think about the two halves:

  • Attention mixes across positions. Tokens look at each other.
  • MLP mixes across features. Each token does some arithmetic on its own newly-informed vector, computing richer features from the components.

Together, attention + MLP, with some bookkeeping (normalisation, residual connections), form one transformer block.

A transformer block reads a sequence of token vectors, enriches them with attention, then refines them with the MLP, then hands the result to the next layer.
faces_html.technical:
A transformer block applied to the residual stream:

$$h' = h + \text{Attn}(\text{LN}(h))$$

$$h'' = h' + \text{MLP}(\text{LN}(h'))$$

The MLP is a position-wise two-layer feed-forward network with a non-linearity (typically GELU): $\text{MLP}(x) = \text{GELU}(x W_{\text{in}} + b_{\text{in}})\, W_{\text{out}} + b_{\text{out}}$, with $W_{\text{in}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 4d}$, $W_{\text{out}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4d \times d}$.

The two halves have distinct roles:

  • Attention mixes across positions (each output depends on all previous inputs).
  • MLP mixes across features at a single position (each output depends only on the corresponding input).

The combination is what makes transformers expressive. A pure attention model has no per-position non-linearity; a pure MLP model has no positional mixing. Both are needed.

Mechanism 4 of 4. Names the attention + MLP partnership and the
responsibility split. The "attention mixes across positions, MLP
mixes across features" line is the key articulation — even
technical audiences who know transformers tend to find this a
useful framing.

No figure (per build constraint). General face stays at the

Beat 3 has now introduced all four mechanisms. The next card
closes the beat.

slides.title: Transformer Stack Summary
slides.body_html:
Beat 3 closes. The function class is now specified:

$$p_\theta(x_{n+1} \mid x_{\le n}) = \text{softmax}\bigl(W_U\, \text{LN}(h_n^{(L)})\bigr)$$

where $h^{(0)} = W_E[x] + W_P[\text{positions}]$, and

$$h^{(l+1)} = h^{(l)} + \text{Attn}(\text{LN}(h^{(l)})) + \text{MLP}(\text{LN}(h^{(l)} + \text{Attn}(\text{LN}(h^{(l)}))))$$

for $l = 0, \ldots, L-1$.

For GPT-2 small: $L = 12$, $d = 768$, $h = 12$, $d_h = 64$, $|V| = 50{,}257$. For frontier models the constants are larger but the form is the same.

The $\theta$ parameters consist of: $W_E$, $W_P$, the per-block $(W_Q^k, W_K^k, W_V^k, W_O, W_{\text{in}}, W_{\text{out}})$, the LN parameters, and $W_U$. About 124M of them for GPT-2 small; 100B+ for the deployed frontier.

faces_html.general:
Beat 3 closes.

Tokens become integers (tokenisation). Integers become vectors (embedding). Vectors read each other (attention). Each layer refines the result (transformer block).

Stack twelve of these blocks (more, for bigger models). Each layer's output is the next layer's input. By the top of the stack, the vector at each position has been mixed, refined, re-mixed, re-refined — twelve times.

The vector at the top represents not just the token, but the token as it appears in this specific context.

From there, one final step (the "unembedding"): map the top vector back to a probability distribution over the vocabulary. That is the next-token distribution we have been chasing since beat 2.

slides.title: Architecture Pipeline
slides.body_html:
Forward pass:

  • Tokenise: $x_{1:n}$ from raw bytes.
  • Embed: $h^{(0)} = W_E[x_{1:n}] + W_P[1{:}n]$, shape $n \times d$.
  • Block stack ($L$ blocks): $h^{(l+1)} = \text{block}(h^{(l)})$, preserving the $n \times d$ shape.
  • Final layer norm: $h_{\text{final}} = \text{LN}(h^{(L)})$.
  • Unembedding: $\text{logits} = h_{\text{final}}\, W_U$, shape $n \times |V|$.
  • Softmax (per-position): yields $p(x_{i+1} \mid x_{\le i})$ for every $i$ in the sequence (used at training time; at inference, only the last position is sampled).

The architecture is parameter-rich and computation-rich but structurally simple — the same block applied $L$ times. There is no recurrence, no convolution, no skip-skip-skip interconnect; just a linear chain of identical residual blocks on a residual stream.

faces_html.general:
The whole machine, in one breath:

  1. Text comes in.
  2. Tokeniser converts it to integer ids.
  3. Each id becomes a 768-dimensional vector (embedding).
  4. Vectors flow through twelve transformer blocks. Each block mixes information across positions (attention) and across features (MLP).
  5. The final vector at the last position becomes a probability distribution over the 50,000-token vocabulary.
  6. Sample one. Append. Go back to step 1.

No outline of what the answer should be. No memory of previous conversations except what is in the prompt. No plan. Just six steps, billions of times.

slides.title: Architecture Scale
slides.body_html:
Parameter accounting for GPT-2 small (~124M parameters total):

  • Embedding $W_E$: $|V| \times d = 50{,}257 \times 768 \approx 38.6\text{M}$.
  • Positional embedding $W_P$: $n_{\text{ctx}} \times d = 1024 \times 768 \approx 0.8\text{M}$.
  • Per-block: 4 attention projections ($Q, K, V, O$) at $768 \times 768 \approx 2.4\text{M}$; MLP $W_{\text{in}}$ ($768 \times 3072$) and $W_{\text{out}}$ ($3072 \times 768$) $\approx 4.7\text{M}$; small LN params. ~7M per block.
  • 12 blocks: ~85M.
  • LN final + unembedding (often tied with $W_E$): negligible additional with weight tying.

Per-block split: ~1/3 attention, ~2/3 MLP. This ratio is consistent across most modern transformer architectures and motivates a separate beat on what the MLP is doing (not in this composition; available as a deeper branch in longer renderings).

Frontier models ($10^{11}$ to $10^{12}$ parameters) keep the same architectural shape and grow $d$, $L$, $|V|$, and $n_{\text{ctx}}$.

faces_html.general:
The pipeline is structurally simple. So why do these models feel so capable?

Because the pipeline is huge.

GPT-2, the model from 2019 that the slides have been talking about, has 124 million parameters. The frontier models in 2026 are in the 100-billion to trillion-parameter range.

Think of every parameter as a tiny knob — a single number, typically a few digits long — that the model multiplies things by during the forward pass. There are 124 million of those knobs in GPT-2. Every time you ask a question, every one of those knobs is consulted, billions of times, to compute the answer.

The architectural choices (attention, MLP, residual stream) make the function class expressive. The scale of parameters makes that expressive function class useful.

Both are needed. The next beat is about how the values of those knobs get set.

slides.title: Compute Overview
slides.body_html:
Compute regimes for an LLM:

  • Training: $O(P \times D)$ FLOPs (Kaplan/Chinchilla scaling). For a 100B-parameter model on 2T tokens, $\sim\!10^{24}$ FLOPs total. Modern training runs use $10^4$ to $10^5$ GPUs in parallel (data + tensor + pipeline parallelism), running for weeks to months.
  • Inference: $O(P)$ FLOPs per generated token (with the KV cache, otherwise $O(P + n_{\text{seq}} \cdot d)$). Latency is typically memory-bandwidth-bound on modern GPUs; the model weights are streamed through the accelerator on each forward pass.

Cost per inference token has dropped roughly $10\times$ per year for several years; cost per training token has not.

faces_html.general:
Worth saying out loud: this only works because of the compute.

Two regimes to keep separate:

  • Training compute. A one-time cost. Months of runtime on thousands of GPUs. Tens of millions of dollars for a frontier model.
  • Inference compute. An ongoing cost. Every time you ask a chatbot a question, the whole machine runs forward, once per token. Most of the per-query cost is here.

Different shapes; different bottlenecks; different economics. The architecture is the same in both regimes; it is the workflow that differs.

slides.title: Compute Training
slides.body_html:
Training compute decomposition.

Per step: forward pass + backward pass + optimiser step. Forward FLOPs $\approx 2PB$ (two FLOPs per parameter per token, where $B$ is batch size). Backward $\approx 2 \times$ forward (two matrix products per layer to compute gradients). Total per-step $\approx 6PB$.

Total training: $\approx 6PD$ where $D$ is total tokens. For $P = 5 \times 10^{11}$, $D = 5 \times 10^{12}$: $\approx 1.5 \times 10^{25}$ FLOPs.

Parallelism strategies:

  • Data parallel: same model, batch sharded.
  • Tensor parallel: each weight matrix sharded across GPUs.
  • Pipeline parallel: layers split across GPUs.

Frontier runs use all three. GPU utilisation is the limiting factor; achieving 50% MFU (model FLOPs utilisation) on a distributed training run is considered good.

faces_html.general:
What does it actually take to train one of these?

Take a frontier-class model — say, 500 billion parameters, trained on a few trillion tokens. The math:

  • Each training step processes a batch of tokens through the model. The forward pass is a few trillion floating-point multiplications.
  • The backward pass — which computes how to nudge each parameter — is roughly the same cost again.
  • You do this billions of times.

All in: 10^24-10^25 floating-point operations. A single fast GPU does 10^15 operations per second. That is 30+ years of GPU time per training run.

Which is why frontier training is done on tens of thousands of GPUs running in parallel for several months. The hardware is half the difficulty.

slides.title: Compute Autodiff
slides.body_html:
How does training "nudge each parameter in the right direction"? Auto-differentiation.

Given a forward pass that computes $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = f_n \circ f_{n-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1\,(\text{input}, \theta)$, reverse-mode auto-diff computes the gradient $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \theta$ in time and memory comparable to the forward pass. The chain rule is applied node-by-node, backwards through the computation graph.

Frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) build the computation graph during the forward pass (or trace it ahead-of-time) and traverse it in reverse. Each operation has a registered backward pass; the gradient propagates layer-by-layer, accumulating contributions from each parameter use.

Cost: $O(\text{forward pass})$, regardless of parameter dimension. Memory: $O(\text{activations})$, which can be reduced via gradient checkpointing (recompute selected forward activations during backward).

Without auto-diff, training a billion-parameter model would require billions of forward passes per gradient step. With auto-diff, a single forward + backward suffices.

slides.title: Compute Inference
slides.body_html:
Per-token inference cost: $\sim 2P$ FLOPs (forward only) plus attention work $O(L \cdot n_{\text{seq}} \cdot d)$ where $n_{\text{seq}}$ grows during decoding.

Bottleneck on modern accelerators: memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. The weight matrices have to be streamed through the accelerator on each forward pass; arithmetic is fast enough that the chip waits on memory. This drives the quantisation push (int8, int4) — fewer bytes per parameter means faster streaming, even though arithmetic ops are cheaper than they need to be.

The KV cache is the standard optimisation: keys and values for prior positions are cached after first computation, so each new token only pays attention cost over the cache, not $O(n^2)$ recomputation. Memory cost: $2 \cdot L \cdot n \cdot d_h \cdot h$ bytes per sequence position.

faces_html.general:
Inference is what happens every time you talk to a chatbot.

To produce one token of output: the entire model runs forward, once. To produce token N+1: the entire model runs forward again, with the prefix one token longer. To produce a 300-token answer: 300 forward passes.

This is why long answers visibly stream in. Each token is a separate computation, and each takes a non-trivial amount of time. Latency scales with model size (bigger = slower per pass) and with how much context the model has to read each pass.

Each user query is, computationally, a full re-run of the machine. There is no shortcut. The economics of operating an LLM service are downstream of this fact.

slides.title: Compute Kv Cache
slides.body_html:
The KV cache, in detail.

During auto-regressive decoding, for each new token at position $n+1$:

  • The new token's $Q_{n+1}$, $K_{n+1}$, $V_{n+1}$ are computed from its embedding.
  • The new token attends to all positions $j \le n+1$.
  • Crucially, $K_j$ and $V_j$ for $j \le n$ were already computed during prior decoding steps and do not change.

The KV cache stores $(K_j, V_j)$ for all prior positions, per layer, per head. On each new token: append the new $K$ and $V$, then run attention with $Q_{n+1}$ against the full cache.

Per-step cost: $O(n)$ instead of $O(n^2)$. Memory cost: $2 \cdot L \cdot n \cdot h \cdot d_h \cdot \text{sizeof(float)}$ per sequence. For long contexts ($32\text{k}{+}$ tokens) on large models, KV cache memory can dominate the parameter memory.

Recent research (group-query attention, multi-query attention) shrinks the cache by sharing K/V across heads. Frontier models use these techniques heavily.

slides.title: Training Objective
slides.body_html:
Pretraining minimises cross-entropy on next-token prediction:

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = - \mathbb{E}_{i \sim \text{corpus}} \left[ \log p_\theta(x_i \mid x_{<i}) \right]$$

The corpus is a concatenation of preprocessed text from web crawl (CommonCrawl filtered), Wikipedia, books, code repositories, scientific papers, etc. Total size: $10^{12}$ to $10^{13}$ tokens for frontier models.

Optimisation is SGD with momentum, in practice Adam(W). Batch sizes are large (millions of tokens per step), implemented via data + tensor + pipeline parallelism across thousands of GPUs. Training a frontier model is a multi-month, multi- million-dollar capital investment.

The objective is self-supervised: no human labels, no auxiliary task. The supervision signal is the next token itself, available at every position in the training corpus.

faces_html.general:
All of this — the embeddings, the attention, the MLP layers — is initialised with random numbers. A freshly built LLM is incoherent. It would predict random tokens, with no structure.

Training is the procedure that turns the random initialisation into a useful model. It works like this:

Show the model a chunk of text. Ask it to predict the next token. Look at what it predicted versus what the actual next token was. Use that error to nudge every parameter slightly, in the direction that would have made the prediction more correct.

Repeat this — trillions of times — across a corpus that is roughly the readable internet: web pages, books, papers, forums, code, manuals.

No labels. No human annotations. The data labels itself: the next token in the text is always the answer. We just hide it, let the model guess, and use the gap as feedback.

This is called self-supervised learning, and at this scale, it is what produces everything you have ever experienced from a chatbot.

slides.title: Training Emergence
slides.body_html:
"Emergence" is the empirical observation that, given enough parameters, enough data, and enough compute, gradient descent on next-token cross-entropy reliably produces parameter configurations that encode multiple levels of linguistic and factual structure — without those structures being part of the optimisation objective.

Concrete observables:

  • Linear probes on intermediate activations recover grammatical features (part of speech, tense, number).
  • Attention head specialisation: heads can be identified that consistently track coreference, syntactic dependency, or named-entity proximity.
  • MLP neuron sparsity: per token, only ~3-5% of MLP intermediate units fire strongly; identified neurons can sometimes be associated with specific concepts (e.g. "code-comment-style," "named-landmark").
  • Probing for factual knowledge ("the capital of France is") shows reliable retrieval up to model-size limits.

None of these properties was directly optimised for. They are downstream consequences of next-token prediction at scale.

Caveat: "emergence" sometimes refers to the more specific claim that capabilities appear suddenly with scale (as opposed to gradually). That stronger claim is contested methodologically (Schaeffer et al. 2023). The weaker claim used here — that next-token-relevant structure ends up encoded — is robust.

faces_html.general:
Here is the part that surprises people.

Nobody designed the embedding clusters where animals end up near each other. Nobody designed the attention head that disambiguates "bank." Nobody designed the MLP neurons that fire on Eiffel-Tower- shaped contexts.

Those structures emerged. They were not built; they were found. The only thing that was specified was: "predict the next token, well, on a lot of text."

The architecture is expressive enough that if there are statistical regularities in the data that help predict the next token, gradient descent will tend to find them. And in natural-language text, there are: grammar, word meaning, syntactic structure, factual associations, coherence, idiom, register, even a notion of arithmetic.

All of those end up encoded — somewhere, in some distributed-and-not-quite-readable way — in the parameters of the trained model.

This is what people mean when they say LLMs are "trained, not programmed." Nothing about the model's behaviour was programmed. All of it was learned, from one objective.

  • Linear probes on intermediate activations recover grammatical features (part of speech, tense, number).
  • Attention head specialisation: heads can be identified that consistently track coreference, syntactic dependency, or named-entity proximity.
  • MLP neuron sparsity: per token, only ~3-5% of MLP intermediate units fire strongly; identified neurons can sometimes be associated with specific concepts (e.g. "code-comment-style," "named-landmark").
  • Probing for factual knowledge ("the capital of France is") shows reliable retrieval up to model-size limits.

None of these properties was directly optimised for. They are downstream consequences of next-token prediction at scale.

Caveat: "emergence" sometimes refers to the more specific claim that capabilities appear suddenly with scale (as opposed to gradually). That stronger claim is contested methodologically (Schaeffer et al. 2023). The weaker claim used here — that next-token-relevant structure ends up encoded — is robust.

slides.title: Alignment Gap
slides.body_html:
The base model after pretraining is $\pi_{\text{base}} = p_{\theta_{\text{base}}}$, a conditional next-token distribution over $V^*$. Sampling from it given a question-shaped prompt does not reliably produce answer-shaped responses, because the training distribution contains many continuations of question-shaped text that are not answers (forum threads, articles, lecture transcripts, metadiscussion).

The misalignment is at the distribution level: the likelihood-maximising continuation under the training distribution is not the user-preferred continuation. No amount of cleverer prompting fixes this without changing the model; the base model is doing exactly what its objective rewards.

faces_html.general:
One last thing. The model we have just described — call it the base model — is not what you talk to.

Ask the base model: "How do I make pancakes?"

The base model has been trained on text where that question appears, and it predicts the next token by the same statistical process as before. The most likely continuation is not necessarily a pancake recipe. It might be:

"How do I make pancakes?" is a common question, especially among first-time cooks. In this article we'll discuss the basic ingredients...

Because in the training data, that question is often followed by more text about the question, not by an answer.

The base model is good at continuing text. It is not yet good at responding to text. That is a different skill, and it is not something the next-token-prediction objective directly selects for.

slides.title: Alignment Thesis
slides.body_html:
Post-training, schematically:

  • SFT: minimise $-\mathbb{E}[\log \pi(\text{response} \mid \text{prompt})]$ on a curated $(\text{prompt}, \text{response})$ dataset of size $10^4$-$10^5$. Yields $\pi_{\text{SFT}}$.
  • Reward model: train $r_\phi(\text{response} \mid \text{prompt})$ from human preference pairs $(\text{resp}_w, \text{resp}_l)$ using a Bradley-Terry-style loss.
  • RLHF (PPO or DPO variants): optimise

$$\pi_{\text{RLHF}} = \arg\max_\pi\, \mathbb{E}[r_\phi(\text{resp})] - \beta\, \text{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_{\text{SFT}})$$

The KL regulariser anchors $\pi_{\text{RLHF}}$ to the SFT reference, preventing reward-model exploitation and preserving general capabilities.

$\pi_{\text{RLHF}}$ is the deployed chatbot. The base predictor is structurally still inside (the architecture hasn't changed, most parameter values haven't moved much), but the distribution over responses has been re-shaped to match human preferences over an answer-formatted style.

The thesis, formally: a deployed LLM-driven chatbot is $\pi_{\text{RLHF}}$, where $\pi_{\text{RLHF}}$ is $\pi_{\text{SFT}}(\pi_{\text{base}})$ shaped by $r_\phi$, where $\pi_{\text{base}}$ is fitted by SGD on next-token cross-entropy over a $\sim\!10^{13}$-token corpus, where the architecture is a stack of $L$ (attention + MLP) residual blocks.

That whole sentence is the artefact. Everything else — the chatbot UI, the system prompt, the safety filtering — is the product layer.

*(Reflexive close, optional: the audience has just watched a $\pi_{\text{RLHF}}$ explain $\pi_{\text{RLHF}}$. The talk performs what it argues. Land if the room has earned it; skip if the room is cold.)*

faces_html.general:
The gap is closed by post-training. Two stages:

  1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT). A team of humans writes a few thousand example (question, answer) pairs, in the register users actually want — direct, helpful, formatted like an answer. The base model is fine-tuned on these pairs. It learns "when text looks like a question, the continuation should look like an answer."
  1. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The fine-tuned model generates pairs of candidate responses; humans pick which they prefer. Those preferences are turned into a reward signal, and the model is fine-tuned again — this time toward responses humans prefer.

Post-training is a thin layer compared to pretraining: a few thousand to a few hundred thousand examples, not a few trillion tokens. The base model is still inside; alignment is a final shaping step.

And that step is the difference between "a probability calculator that emits internet-flavoured text" and "a chatbot that answers your question."

That is the talk.

A modern LLM is a probability calculator that emits one token at a time. Everything that makes it feel like a thinking entity — fluency, context, factual recall — is the joint work of a stack of mechanisms (tokenisation, embedding, attention, transformer block) trained at internet scale, then nudged by a thin alignment layer at the very end.

The calculator is the body; the mechanisms are the limbs; training is the upbringing; alignment is the manners.
